messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 43
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Plumber
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 79

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smoke): Smoke or fire smell, Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid All Feelings: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Threat: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Vignette:
Asha was 43, married, and had spent most of her adult life doing plumbing work in other people’s homes and in the apartment buildings around her neighborhood, where her days were usually noisy, physical, and practical. Before the incident, she was known as someone who could work calmly in cramped basements and behind old kitchen walls, moving through spaces that others found unpleasant without much comment. That changed after a job in an older building where a hidden leak had damaged insulation and exposed a toxic chemical source. As she worked, a sharp, burnt odor had drifted through the space, and then the scene became confused and dangerous in the way she still struggled to put into words: the smell lingered, her body reacted immediately, and the job site that had seemed ordinary became the place she now remembered as the start of everything that followed. The smell was not just unpleasant to her; it had become tied to the moment she realized something was seriously wrong, and even now she could still recall how the burnt scent seemed to fill the whole room and cling to her clothes and hair.

In the weeks after that exposure, Asha found that certain smells could pull her straight back into the experience. Smoke from a neighbor’s cooking, the faint odor of a fireplace, or any burnt smell in the air could make her stop mid-sentence and turn her head as if she needed to confirm where it was coming from. Related smells, even when they were only vaguely similar, unsettled her. She described them as “the kind of smell that tells you something’s wrong before you can think.” At work, this meant that ordinary assignments became harder to tolerate. She would notice a smell before anyone else seemed to, and once she noticed it, she could not easily let it go. In homes where something had been left too long on the stove or in buildings with older wiring, she became tense and preoccupied, scanning for the source rather than settling into the task in front of her.

Over time, Asha began organizing her days around avoiding anything that might stir up strong feelings of any kind. She had come to believe that if she let herself feel too much—fear, sadness, anger, even excitement—she might lose control of her reactions or become overwhelmed by the memories. So she tried to keep her life narrowed down to what was necessary. She stayed busy, kept conversations brief, and declined invitations if she thought the setting might leave her emotionally exposed. Even positive moments felt risky to her because they could be followed by a crash she did not want to experience. Her husband noticed that she had become harder to read, but Asha described it as a way of keeping herself contained. She did not trust her own internal reactions and preferred not to give them room.

She also developed a habit of constantly checking her surroundings. In every house, hallway, store, or parking lot, she was on the lookout for signs of threat, especially anything that might suggest smoke, heat, or danger nearby. On the job she would glance toward ovens, utility closets, and vents more often than before, and in public places she positioned herself so she could see exits and other people around her. This watchfulness had become automatic. Even at home, she found herself looking around the kitchen or toward the windows without realizing she was doing it. At night, she woke repeatedly to check whether she was safe. She would listen, sit up, and look around the bedroom before allowing herself to lie back down, only to wake again later and repeat the same routine. The interruption left her tired, but it also felt necessary to her, as though sleep could not be trusted without verification.

Medical settings became increasingly difficult for her. She avoided hospitals, ambulances, and physical examinations, not because she had a planned explanation for doing so, but because those places and procedures felt too close to the memory of being medically vulnerable after the exposure. She delayed appointments, found reasons not to go, and preferred to manage discomfort herself whenever possible. The thought of lying on a table, being examined, or walking past emergency equipment made her tense before she even arrived. As a result, she missed routine care and created tension at home when her husband urged her to be checked. She recognized that the avoidance was narrowing her options, yet the idea of entering those settings felt worse to her than postponing them.

What finally brought Asha to seek help was the accumulation of these changes. She was exhausted from sleeping lightly, from scanning every room, and from bracing herself whenever a smoke or burnt smell appeared. At work, she had become so alert to odor cues that she could not relax long enough to complete some jobs without repeated pauses, and she worried about how visible her distress had become. She came in now because she no longer wanted her days arranged around keeping herself on guard. What she feared most was that a familiar smell might hit her unexpectedly and send her body into the same intense reaction again; what she hoped for was some way to move through her home and her work without feeling that she had to check, watch, and hold herself back at every turn.
